lessons.title: Case Study: Three Indian Taxpayers, Three Different Choices

children.text: Time to put the whole course to work. Three salaried Indians, one tax year, three different answers. Follow each from the April declaration to the July filing, including the surprises that show up in between. By the end you should be able to run this for yourself without looking anything up.

cells: Salaried product manager plus freelance consulting

body.title: Tax Under Each Regime, Before Capital Gains (₹ Thousand)

children.text: Meera: Nil Tax, and a Family That Disagrees

Meera earns ₹9,80,000 with a basic of ₹4,00,000 and HRA of ₹1,60,000, and pays ₹12,000 a month rent in Coimbatore. Her EPF is ₹48,000, her health policy costs ₹12,000 and Tamil Nadu professional tax takes ₹2,500. In April her father urges her to declare the old regime and start an ELSS SIP.

HRA exemption: least of ₹1,60,000 received, rent ₹1,44,000 minus 10% of basic ₹40,000 (₹1,04,000), and 40% of basic (₹1,60,000). Exemption ₹1,04,000. Benefits: ₹1,04,000 plus ₹48,000, ₹12,000 and ₹2,500, which is ₹1,66,500.
New regime: ₹9,80,000 minus ₹75,000 is ₹9,05,000, below ₹12 lakh, so tax is nil. To match that in the old regime she would need benefits of ₹4,30,000, about two and a half times what she has.

At filing, her AIS shows ₹18,000 of FD interest and ₹6,000 of savings interest. New regime taxable income becomes ₹9,29,000, still below ₹12 lakh, so her tax stays nil. She must still report the interest in her return.

body.text: Meera's decision took thirty seconds: her salary is below ₹12.75 lakh, so the new regime cannot be beaten. The ELSS SIP her father suggested would have bought her nothing in tax. She started one anyway, in a plain index fund with no lock-in, because she wants equity exposure for a goal ten years away.

children.text: Rajat: The Mumbai Rent That Pays for Itself

Rajat earns ₹38,00,000 with a basic of ₹15,20,000 and HRA of ₹7,60,000, and pays ₹85,000 a month for a flat in Chembur. He maxes 80C and 80CCD(1B), pays ₹75,000 of health insurance covering his senior-citizen parents, and ₹2,500 of Maharashtra professional tax. In November he also sells equity mutual fund units, booking ₹4,00,000 of long-term capital gains.

HRA exemption: least of ₹7,60,000 received, rent ₹10,20,000 minus 10% of basic ₹1,52,000 (₹8,68,000), and 50% of basic for Mumbai (₹7,60,000). Exemption ₹7,60,000. Benefits: ₹7,60,000 plus ₹1,50,000, ₹50,000, ₹75,000 and ₹2,500, which is ₹10,37,500.

New regime: ₹38,00,000 minus ₹75,000 is ₹37,25,000. Tax is ₹3,00,000 plus 30% of ₹13,25,000 (₹3,97,500), total ₹6,97,500, plus ₹27,900 cess, which is ₹7,25,400. The old regime wins by ₹74,100, exactly the ₹2,37,500 by which his benefits exceed the ₹8 lakh breakeven, multiplied by 0.312.

Capital gains: ₹4,00,000 minus the ₹1,25,000 annual exemption is ₹2,75,000, taxed at 12.5%, which is ₹34,375 in either regime. Old regime total: ₹6,26,250 plus ₹34,375 is ₹6,60,625, plus ₹26,425 cess, which is ₹6,87,050. New regime total: ₹6,97,500 plus ₹34,375 is ₹7,31,875, plus ₹29,275 cess, which is ₹7,61,150. Neither regime's taxable income crosses ₹50 lakh, so no surcharge applies, and the old regime still wins by ₹74,100.

body.text: Notice what the capital gains did to Rajat's decision: nothing. They are taxed identically in both regimes, so they change his tax bill but not his choice. He declares the old regime in April, submits rent receipts with his landlord's PAN in January, and files ITR-2 because of the capital gains.

body.title: Rajat Buys a Flat
body.prompt: Next year Rajat buys a flat in Thane, stops paying rent and pays ₹2,00,000 of home loan interest. His salary and other deductions are unchanged, so his benefits become ₹4,77,500. If he stubbornly stays in the old regime, how much more tax does he pay than under the new regime? Ignore capital gains.
body.explanation: Old regime taxable income becomes ₹38,00,000 minus ₹50,000 minus ₹4,77,500, which is ₹32,72,500. Tax is ₹1,12,500 plus 30% of ₹22,72,500 (₹6,81,750), total ₹7,94,250, plus ₹31,770 cess, which is ₹8,26,020. New regime tax stays ₹7,25,400. Staying in the old regime would cost him ₹1,00,620 more. Losing HRA flips a comfortable old regime win into a large loss.

children.text: Sanjana: A Side Business Changes the Rules

Sanjana earns ₹16,00,000 with a basic of ₹6,40,000 and HRA of ₹2,56,000, pays ₹28,000 a month rent in Bengaluru, maxes 80C, pays ₹25,000 for health insurance and ₹2,500 of Karnataka professional tax. She also bills ₹4,00,000 a year consulting for two startups, which she reports under presumptive taxation at 50%, giving ₹2,00,000 of professional income.

HRA exemption: least of ₹2,56,000 received, rent ₹3,36,000 minus 10% of basic ₹64,000 (₹2,72,000), and 40% of basic for Bengaluru (₹2,56,000). Exemption ₹2,56,000. Benefits: ₹2,56,000 plus ₹1,50,000, ₹25,000 and ₹2,500, which is ₹4,33,500.

Old regime: salary income is ₹16,00,000 minus ₹50,000, ₹2,56,000 and ₹2,500, which is ₹12,91,500. Adding ₹2,00,000 of professional income gives ₹14,91,500, and subtracting ₹1,50,000 under 80C and ₹25,000 under 80D leaves ₹13,16,500. Tax is ₹1,12,500 plus 30% of ₹3,16,500 (₹94,950), total ₹2,07,450, plus ₹8,298 cess, which is ₹2,15,748.

New regime: ₹16,00,000 minus ₹75,000 is ₹15,25,000, plus ₹2,00,000 of professional income, which is ₹17,25,000. Tax is ₹1,20,000 plus 20% of ₹1,25,000 (₹25,000), total ₹1,45,000, plus ₹5,800 cess, which is ₹1,50,800. The new regime wins by ₹64,948.

body.text: Sanjana's consulting fees are professional income, so she no longer gets a free yearly choice. Here the new regime wins comfortably anyway, so she simply stays in it, files ITR-4 and keeps her one-time exit unused. Had the old regime won by a small margin, she would have had to weigh one year of savings against giving up that flexibility for the rest of her freelancing career.

body.title: Which Rule Applies to Sanjana?
body.question: Sanjana decides in tax year 2027-28 that the old regime is finally better for her. What must she do, assuming she still has consulting income?
options: Simply tick the opt-out question in her return, like any salaried person
File the prescribed option form before the return due date, and remember she can come back to the new regime only once
Nothing, since she can no longer choose the old regime at all
Ask her employer to switch her regime in Form 16
body.explanation: With business or professional income, opting out requires the prescribed form filed before the due date, and the return journey to the new regime can be made only once. Her employer's Form 16 has no bearing on her final regime.

events.title: Declarations to payroll
events.description: Meera declares the new regime and ignores the family advice. Rajat declares the old regime with his rent and investment details. Sanjana declares the new regime, which is also the default.

events.title: Mid-year events
events.description: Rajat books ₹4 lakh of long-term gains on equity funds, which changes his tax but not his regime. Sanjana's consulting billing reaches ₹4 lakh, confirming she is in the business-income rules.

events.title: Proof submission
events.description: Rajat uploads rent receipts, his landlord's PAN, 80C proofs and health insurance receipts, so his TDS stays accurate. Meera and Sanjana have nothing to prove.

events.title: Form 16 and AIS
events.description: All three reconcile Form 16 with AIS. Meera finds ₹24,000 of interest income she had forgotten.

events.title: Filing
events.description: Meera files ITR-1 with nil tax, Rajat files ITR-2 under the old regime, and Sanjana files ITR-4 under the new regime. All three e-verify the same day.

body.title: Your Turn: Advise Ishita
body.scenario: Ishita, 33, is a Delhi-based architect on a salary of ₹13,20,000, with a basic of ₹5,28,000 and HRA of ₹2,64,000. She pays ₹25,000 a month rent in Saket, fills 80C to ₹1,50,000 through EPF and PPF, and pays ₹22,800 for health insurance. Delhi levies no professional tax. She also has ₹40,000 of long-term gains from equity funds and no business income.
body.prompt: Work out both regimes and tell her which to choose, and why.
body.modelAnswer: HRA exemption is the least of ₹2,64,000 received, rent ₹3,00,000 minus 10% of basic ₹52,800 (₹2,47,200), and 50% of basic for Delhi (₹2,64,000), so ₹2,47,200. Benefits are ₹2,47,200 plus ₹1,50,000 and ₹22,800, which is ₹4,20,000. Old regime taxable income is ₹13,20,000 minus ₹50,000 minus ₹4,20,000, which is ₹8,50,000. Tax is ₹12,500 plus 20% of ₹3,50,000 (₹70,000), total ₹82,500, plus ₹3,300 cess, which is ₹85,800. New regime taxable income is ₹12,45,000. Slab tax is ₹60,000 plus 15% of ₹45,000 (₹6,750), which is ₹66,750, but marginal relief caps tax at the ₹45,000 excess over ₹12 lakh, so it is ₹45,000 plus ₹1,800 cess, which is ₹46,800. Her ₹40,000 of long-term gains is within the ₹1.25 lakh annual exemption, so it is untaxed in both regimes. The new regime wins by ₹39,000, largely thanks to marginal relief. As a salaried taxpayer with no business income she can revisit this next year, and should, since a rent increase or a home loan would change the answer.

body.title: The One-Word Predictor
body.textWithBlank: Across all our examples, the single benefit that most often decides whether the old regime can win is the ___ exemption.
body.explanation: Without a large HRA exemption, common deductions rarely add up to the breakeven. Rajat wins with a ₹7,60,000 HRA exemption and loses that edge the moment he buys a home.

body.text: There is no better regime. There is only the regime that fits your income, your rent, your loans and your year, recalculated every April and confirmed every July.

body.title: Do This Within the Next Week
steps: Pull your latest payslip and note basic, HRA and any employer NPS contribution
Total your genuine old regime benefits beyond the ₹50,000 standard deduction
Compare that total with the breakeven for your salary from Chapter 3
Check your AIS for interest, dividends and capital gains you may have forgotten
Confirm your payroll declaration matches the regime your numbers support
Ask HR whether employer NPS at 14% of basic is available to you
Diarise 15 July next year to file and e-verify on the same day

points: Below about ₹12.75 lakh of salary, the new regime wins by default and no amount of tax-saving changes that.
High earners paying large metro rents are the clearest old regime candidates, and they lose that edge the moment the rent stops.
Capital gains are taxed identically in both regimes, so they change your tax bill but not your regime choice.
Any business or professional income, however small, replaces the yearly choice with one exit and one return.
Marginal relief just above ₹12 lakh can decide the outcome for mid-salary taxpayers.
Run the comparison every April with realistic numbers, confirm it every July with Form 16 and AIS, and file on time.

body.text: That is the whole course. You can now calculate tax under both regimes, find your breakeven, spot the traps around ₹12 lakh, ₹50 lakh and capital gains, declare correctly to your employer and file with confidence. The rules will keep changing with each Union Budget. The method you have learned here will not.

This lesson is for education only and is not tax or investment advice. All three taxpayers are illustrative, and figures reflect the rules applicable to tax year 2026-27 as understood at the time of writing, for residents without surcharge. Consult a qualified tax professional before filing.
